en: The Sūtra on Anāthapiṇḍada’s Conversion of His Seven Sons, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master An Shigao of Parthia during the Later Han Dynasty.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Bhagavat was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, the Garden of Anāthapiṇḍada.

"Ānanda, at that time Anāthapiṇḍika had seven sons who lacked firm faith in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha. They did not take refuge in the Buddha, they did not take refuge in the Dharma, and they did not take refuge in the Bhikṣu-saṅgha. Furthermore, they did not refrain from killing, they did not refrain from taking what was not given, they did not refrain from sexual misconduct, they did not refrain from false speech, and they did not refrain from drinking intoxicants."
At that time, the householder Anāthapiṇḍada said to his seven sons:

"You should now take refuge in the Buddha, take refuge in the Dharma, and take refuge in the Saṅgha of bhikṣus. Furthermore, do not kill living beings; do not take what is not given; do not commit sexual misconduct with the wives of others; do not speak falsely; and do not drink intoxicants—do not transgress against any of these."
That son spoke these words:

"I am not capable of taking refuge in the Buddha, taking refuge in the Dharma, or taking refuge in the Saṅgha of bhikṣus; I am also not capable of refraining from killing, nor from taking what is not given, nor from sexual misconduct, nor from false speech, nor from drinking intoxicants—I am incapable of all these."
The householder Anāthapiṇḍada said:

"I shall grant you a thousand measures of gold; you should take refuge in the Buddha, take refuge in the Dharma, and take refuge in the Saṅgha of Bhikṣus. Reform yourselves by abandoning killing, taking what is not given, sexual misconduct, false speech, and drinking intoxicants—abandon all of these."

At that time, having obtained one thousand measures of gold, the seven sons took refuge in the Buddha, took refuge in the Dharma, and took refuge in the Saṅgha of bhikṣus; they then renounced killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, false speech, and drinking intoxicants.

Then the elder Anāthapiṇḍada, having bestowed one thousand pieces of gold upon each of his seven sons, received the three refuges and the five precepts; he then proceeded to the park where the World-Honored One was staying, prostrated himself at the Buddha’s feet, and sat to one side.
Then Anāthapiṇḍika addressed the World-Honored One, saying:

"I have seven sons here who lack sincere faith and possess no joyful heart toward the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha; they do not take refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Bhikṣu-saṅgha, nor do they refrain from killing, refrain from stealing, refrain from sexual misconduct, refrain from false speech, or refrain from drinking intoxicants."
"World-Honored One!

At that time, you gave each of the seven sons one thousand taels of gold, and caused them to take refuge in the Buddha, take refuge in the Dharma, and take refuge in the Sangha of bhikṣus, while bestowing upon them the five precepts."
"What do you think, World-Honored One?
Do those seven sons possess any merit, goodness, or virtuous qualities that would cause them to obtain something in the future?
The World-Honored One replied:
“Excellent, excellent, householder!
You bring great benefit to sentient beings; you desire to bring peace and security to sentient beings, and gods and humans shall obtain peace.”

"Elder! By virtue of these merits, those seven sons shall be fully endowed with all wholesome qualities. Listen attentively as I now describe the fruits obtained through the various wholesome merits resulting from the causes of those seven sons."

To the north there is a country with a city named Śaila-kuṭī; its lands are fertile and its people are numerous and flourishing. Therein lies the Airāvaṇa-treasury, containing hundreds of thousands of pieces of gold and silver, as well as precious jewels, musāragalva, agate, pearls, amber, crystal, lapis lazuli, and various other exquisite gems.

For seven years, seven months, and seven days, the people of that land of Gandhāra may fill their laps, carry him on their arms, or bear him upon their heads, expending him according to their every desire; yet the treasury of that Airāvaṇa remains undiminished.
Furthermore, householder!

Those seven sons, as well as this great treasure-store of Airāvaṇa and those seven thousand measures of gold—even multiplied a hundredfold, a thousandfold, a hundred-thousandfold, or countless times—cannot equal the merit obtained by your seven sons.

"Elder! Furthermore, there is a country named Kaliṅga and a city named Mithilā, where grain is abundant and the population is flourishing. Therein is a treasure-store named Pañcūpa, containing countless precious things—gold, silver, musāragalva, agate, pearls, crystal, lapis lazuli, coral, amber, and so forth—even down to the people of the Kaliṅga country, who for seven years, seven months, and seven days may carry away as much as they desire according to their wishes, yet it does not diminish; nevertheless, that country of Kaliṅga does suffer depletion."

Furthermore, if the seven sons of the elder possessed seven thousand measures of gold and the great treasure-store of *pañca-pūṭa*, even if those seven thousand measures of gold were multiplied a hundredfold, a thousandfold, a hundred-thousandfold, or countless times, they would all fail to equal the seven thousand measures of gold belonging to the seven sons; the merit obtained [by the elder] is beyond compare.
Furthermore, householder!

In the kingdom of Videha, there is a city named Sūrata. Therein lies the great treasure-store Piṅgala, containing countless hundreds of thousands of precious treasuries—gold, silver, musāragalva, agate, pearls, amber, crystal, and lapis lazuli. Within that kingdom of Videha, for seven years, seven months, and seven days, one may carry away as much as one desires, bearing it all away; yet the Piṅgala treasure-store therein is not diminished at all.

Furthermore, Elder, as for the seven sons’ seven thousand ounces of gold and the Piṅgala treasure-store—these seven thousand ounces of gold, even multiplied a hundredfold, a thousandfold, a hundred-thousandfold, or countless times, would all fail to equal the merit obtained by the seven sons; it is beyond measure and calculation.
Furthermore, householder!

In the city of Vārāṇasī in the kingdom of Kāśi, there is a treasury named the Nāga-karaṇḍa, containing countless gold, silver, precious gems, musāragalva, agate, crystal, lapis lazuli, pearls, and amber. Suppose those seven sons were to have seven thousand measures of gold, and this great treasure-store of the Nāga-karaṇḍa were also theirs; the merit obtained by those seven thousand measures of gold would not equal even a hundredth part, a thousandth part, a hundred-thousandth part, or an incalculable fraction of the merit [of that other].
"Householder!

Setting aside the people of Gandhāra, setting aside the people of Kaliṅga, setting aside the people of Videha, and setting aside the people of Kāśi—even if all the men, women, and children, great and small, from these sixteen great nations of Jambudvīpa were to carry away these four great treasuries of precious things—gold, silver, jewels, musāragalva, agate, pearls, amber, crystal, and lapis lazuli—as much as they desired for seven years, seven months, and seven days, carrying it all away according to their wishes, those four great treasuries would not diminish at all."
"Householder!

Those seven sons’ seven thousand measures of gold, as well as these four great treasuries of jewels, do not equal even a hundredth part, a thousandth part, a hundred-thousandth part, or an incalculable fraction [of this]."
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
“Irāvatī and Gandhārī, Mucilinda and Paṅkadhā,
Piṅgala and Surasā, Sañjaya and Vārāṇasī.”
"These four treasuries of jewels, filled with various kinds of precious gems, are so numerous that they cannot be fully measured;
such is the fruit of the merit one has performed.
At that time, the World-Honored One expounded the subtle and wondrous Dharma to Anāthapiṇḍada, exhorting him until he was filled with joy.

At that time, the householder Anāthapiṇḍada, having heard the subtle and wondrous Dharma from the Tathāgata, rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"I pray that the World-Honored One will accept my invitation for himself and the community of bhikṣus; I wish to provide them with ambrosial food and drink for the sake of those seven sons."
Then the World-Honored One silently accepted Anāthapiṇḍada’s invitation.

Seeing that the World-Honored One had silently accepted his invitation, Anāthapiṇḍada bowed his head at the Buddha’s feet and withdrew. Returning home on that very day, he prepared ambrosial food and drink; having prepared the delicious meal, he spread out the seating mats for the Buddha and the community of bhikṣus and announced that the time had come: "Now is the right time; I pray that the World-Honored One will deign to attend."

At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing that the hour had come, put on his robes and took up his bowl; surrounded by the community of bhikṣus before and behind him, he entered the city of Śrāvastī and went to the house of Anāthapiṇḍada, where he and the community of bhikṣus took their seats.

Then the householder Anāthapiṇḍada and his seven sons went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated themselves at his feet, and sat to one side. At that time, the householder Anāthapiṇḍada addressed the World-Honored One, saying:

"I have these seven sons; I shall each give them a thousand taels of gold so that they may take refuge in the Buddha, take refuge in the Dharma, and take refuge in the Saṅgha of bhikṣus, and cause them to receive the five precepts."
"I now pray that the World-Honored One will preach the Dharma for these people, so that we seven sons may attain right view under the Tathāgata.
Then, the World-Honored One addressed the householder Anāthapiṇḍada, saying:
"So it is, householder!"
"So be it, householder!
Then the householder Anāthapiṇḍada, seeing that the Buddha and the community of bhikṣus were seated, together with his seven sons, provided them with offerings of sweet and choice food and drink.

At that time, the householder Anāthapiṇḍada and his seven sons served delicious food and drink to the Buddha and the community of bhikṣus. When they saw that the World-Honored One had finished eating and had set aside his bowl, the householder Anāthapiṇḍada approached the World-Honored One, prostrated himself at his feet, and sat to one side.

Then the Tathāgata taught the subtle and wondrous Dharma to those seven sons. Knowing that Anāthapiṇḍada’s seven sons were listening to the Dharma with a sincere heart, the World-Honored One—following the teaching that all Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, invariably preach regarding suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path—expounded this Dharma to the seven sons of the elder Anāthapiṇḍada. Instantly, as they sat there, all defilements and impurities were exhausted; free from blemish, they attained the arising of the Dharma-eye.

Having already seen the Dharma, he attained the profound Dharma and was free from doubt; being without hesitation, he conceived a state of fearlessness. Having understood the profound Dharma of the Tathāgata, he took refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha, and received the five precepts.
Then the World-Honored One, having again preached the Dharma extensively for the householder Anāthapiṇḍada and his seven sons, rose from his seat and departed.
At that time, the householder Anāthapiṇḍada and his seven sons, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
The Sūtra on Anāthapiṇḍada’s Conversion of His Seven Sons.
